title: The $313M war chest against the $63M operating burn
body:
## A company measured in losses, not revenues

The simplest way to understand POET Technologies' financial architecture is this: in the fiscal year ended December 31, 2025, the company recorded net losses of $62.96 million against revenues of approximately $1.2 million. The ratio — losses to revenues — was roughly fifty to one. By any conventional operating metric, POET does not yet exist as a going concern in the commercial sense. It exists as a funded thesis.

That distinction matters for how an investor reads every line of the income statement and balance sheet. The revenue figure — $1.2 million, composed entirely of non-recurring engineering receipts and small product deliveries — did not cover a single quarter of POET's $18.08 million annual research and development spend. The quarterly cadence told a consistent story: Q3 2025 contributed $298,000 of revenue; Q4 2025 contributed $341,000. These are engagement revenues — fees paid by prospective customers and development partners to co-develop specific implementations of the POET Optical Interposer — not product line revenues. They mark technical progress, not commercial scale.

The $62.96 million net loss is real money consumed in pursuit of a platform that has not yet shipped at commercial volumes. But to read it purely as destruction of value is to misread the company's stage. The correct frame is: what did POET buy with that $63 million, and does the purchase price look reasonable against the option being underwritten?

## The expense walk: where the cash went

R&D expenditure for FY2025 came in at $18.08 million, of which $2.22 million was stock-based compensation — a non-cash charge that reflects the cost of retaining engineers and scientists against the option of better-compensated roles at established semiconductor firms. The cash component of R&D, approximately $15.86 million, funded the Singapore-based wafer-level photonic integration line and the ongoing qualification work with strategic partners including Sivers Semiconductors.

General and administrative expenses totalled $25.08 million. Within that figure, $3.89 million was stock-based compensation and $3.32 million was depreciation and amortisation — both non-cash. The cash SG&A was therefore closer to $17.87 million, a figure that reflects the costs of maintaining dual NASDAQ-TSX listings, SEC foreign private issuer compliance (20-F filings rather than 10-K), investor relations infrastructure, and a senior management team assembled for a company whose market capitalisation trades on expectations rather than earnings multiples.

Aggregating the non-cash charges — stock-based compensation across R&D and SG&A, plus depreciation and amortisation — produces approximately $35 million of non-cash operating costs in FY2025. Strip those out of the $62.96 million net loss, adjust for working capital movements, and the cash operating burn resolves to approximately $45 million for the year. At that rate, the financial architecture of POET becomes considerably more interesting.

## The balance sheet expansion: $250 million changes everything

At December 31, 2024, POET's total assets stood at $69.7 million, with cash and short-term investments of $53.8 million. Twelve months later, total assets had grown to $328.6 million — a near fivefold expansion — and cash and short-term investments had risen to $313.4 million. Working capital, the conventional measure of short-term financial health, stood at $170.7 million.

The mechanism was a single transaction: a $250 million institutional equity financing closed during FY2025, drawing from three unnamed institutional investors whose identities remained undisclosed at the snapshot date. The raise was structurally significant not merely for the quantum but for what it signalled about institutional conviction in the CPO architectural bet. Raising $250 million into a pre-revenue photonics platform company — at a moment when co-packaged optics remained an engineering debate rather than a commercial standard — required investors willing to price a multi-year option rather than a current earnings stream.

| Balance sheet item | Dec 31, 2024 | Dec 31, 2025 | Change |
|---|---|---|---|
| Total assets (USD millions) | $69.7 | $328.6 | +$258.9M (+372%) |
| Cash & short-term investments | $53.8 | $313.4 | +$259.6M (+483%) |
| Working capital | — | $170.7 | — |
| Derivative warrant liability | — | ($135.6) | — |
| Convertible debt | — | ($5.8) | — |

The balance sheet transformation was not free. Alongside the $313.4 million in cash, POET carried a $135.6 million derivative warrant liability — the mark-to-market fair value of the warrants issued as part of the financing. This is a non-cash accounting item: it moves with POET's share price and does not require current cash settlement. But it represents a real economic obligation. If the warrants are exercised at maturity, the resulting dilution is meaningful, and the liability figure reflects the market's current best estimate of what that exercise will cost existing shareholders.

A smaller convertible debt position of $5.8 million rounded out the liability side. Against the cash position, the net financial picture remained strongly positive — but the derivative warrant liability deserved its own accounting in any serious valuation exercise.

## Runway: seven years of optionality

Divide $313.4 million of cash and short-term investments by $45 million of annual cash burn, and the arithmetic produces approximately seven years of runway at the FY2025 operating rate. For a pre-commercial photonics platform company, this is a structurally unusual and strategically important position.

Most pre-revenue semiconductor and photonics companies operating at comparable R&D intensity carry two to four years of runway — enough to reach a development milestone but not enough to sustain a prolonged qualification cycle if hyperscaler adoption timelines slip. POET's seven-year horizon changes the negotiating posture in customer conversations. A potential OEM or hyperscaler evaluating the Optical Interposer does not need to worry whether POET will be solvent long enough to support a three-year qualification programme. The cash on hand absorbs that concern.

The runway figure also reflects what the institutional investors effectively purchased: not earnings exposure in 2025 or 2026, but the right to be present when co-packaged optics crosses from engineering pilots to volume qualification. If that crossing happens in 2027 or 2028, POET's cash position means it will be at the table regardless of intervening revenue shortfalls.

This calculus only holds if the burn rate stays approximately flat. A significant acceleration in headcount, capital expenditure for expanded manufacturing capacity, or additional investment required to maintain strategic partnerships could compress the runway materially. The $45 million figure reflected FY2025's operating configuration; it was not a ceiling.

## Share structure and the dilution overhang

At December 31, 2025, POET had 132.3 million common shares outstanding. Against that base, the fully diluted share count implied by outstanding options (5.79 million) and warrants (37.36 million) was approximately 175.45 million shares — a potential dilution of 28.35% from the current common share count if all instruments were exercised.

The warrant component carried the larger structural weight. The 37.36 million outstanding warrants linked directly to the $135.6 million derivative warrant liability on the balance sheet. If warrants are exercised as the share price appreciates — the scenario under which they would rationally be exercised — existing shareholders absorb a 28% increase in the share count. In a company trading on option value rather than earnings, that dilution calculus materially affects per-share intrinsic value at any assumed future revenue multiple.

The 5.79 million options represented the more conventional dilution mechanism: management and employee retention instruments whose vesting schedules and strike prices were disclosed in the 20-F footnotes. Their dilutive effect was real but secondary to the warrant structure.

For a sophisticated investor modelling POET's per-share value in a bull case — say, qualification as a component supplier in one or more hyperscaler CPO programmes by 2028 — the analysis required working from the fully diluted count, not the current common share count. The difference between 132.3 million and 175.45 million shares is not trivial at any revenue multiple meaningful enough to justify a significant position.

## The accumulated deficit: what $297 million of patience looks like

POET's accumulated deficit stood at approximately $297 million at the FY2025 close, reflecting the cumulative equity consumed since the company committed to the photonic integration platform thesis. Against that, accumulated net operating losses of approximately $180 million represented the tax-shelter asset embedded in the balance sheet — losses that could, if POET ever reached sustained profitability, shelter a meaningful portion of future taxable income.

The $297 million figure deserves to be read as historical context rather than as an indictment. Semiconductor platform companies — from InPhi to Ayar Labs to Ranovus — typically consume hundreds of millions of dollars before a component architecture reaches the volume qualification stage. POET's cumulative losses, measured against the cost basis of competing platforms developed inside better-capitalised incumbents, were not obviously outsized. What distinguished POET's position from a typical distressed pre-revenue equity was the $313 million cash cushion that, as of the snapshot date, ensured those historical losses would not be the cause of the thesis failing.

The investment question, stated plainly, was not whether POET had burned capital in the past — it unambiguously had, at scale, across more than a decade — but whether the $313 million now on the balance sheet was sufficient to survive to the moment when hyperscaler CPO adoption produced a revenue event meaningful enough to validate the accumulated investment. The financial architecture, as constructed at December 31, 2025, said the answer was probably yes. The technology and market architecture said the answer remained genuinely uncertain.
